title: Maple Syrup vs Honey: Which Has More Sugar and Calories?

seo.title: Maple Syrup vs Honey: Sugar and Calories
seo.meta_description: Honey is more concentrated: about 82 g sugar and 304 calories per 100 g versus roughly 60–67 g sugar and 260 calories for pure maple syrup. A tablespoon of honey is also usually higher.
seo.search_intent: Compare honey and maple syrup for sugar, calories, serving size, and practical use.

excerpt: Honey usually contains more sugar and calories than pure maple syrup both per 100 grams and per tablespoon. Honey is about 82 g sugar and 304 calories per 100 g; maple syrup is roughly 60–67 g and 260 calories.
content_html:
Honey and maple syrup are both concentrated liquid sweeteners, but honey contains less water. That makes honey higher in both sugar and calories than pure maple syrup on a weight basis, and the difference usually remains in a tablespoon serving.

The 100-gram comparison explains concentration, but few people eat 100 grams of either sweetener at once. A tablespoon gives a more realistic picture for oatmeal, toast, yogurt, or a recipe. Even then, the amount you actually pour matters more than the small compositional edge. A generous tablespoon of maple syrup can deliver more sugar than a measured teaspoon of honey, so portion size can easily reverse what a chart seems to imply.

Water content creates another practical difference. Maple syrup is thinner and disperses easily through oatmeal, yogurt, or drinks, while honey is more viscous and may stay concentrated in smaller areas. That changes how sweet a dish tastes and how much someone chooses to add. It is not an inherent health advantage for either sweetener, but it is one reason a nutrient table cannot predict the exact amount that will end up in a real recipe.

If a recipe already contains several sweet ingredients, switching only the syrup may barely change the final sugar total. Looking at the whole dish gives a more realistic picture than focusing on one tablespoon in isolation.

Per 100 grams, honey is more concentrated

Per 100 gTotal sugarsCalories
Honey≈82 g≈304 kcal
Pure maple syrup≈60–67 g≈260 kcal

Honey's sugars are primarily fructose and glucose. Maple syrup contains more water and is dominated by sucrose.

They also behave differently in cooking. Honey is more viscous and contains a mixture rich in fructose and glucose, while pure maple syrup contains more water and is dominated by sucrose. In baking, swapping one for the other can change moisture, browning, and texture. A cup-for-cup replacement is not always neutral. Precision recipes work better when you follow the specified sweetener or adjust other liquids intentionally.

The tablespoon comparison points the same way

One tablespoon of honey weighs about 21 grams and supplies roughly 64 calories and 17 grams of sugar. A tablespoon of maple syrup weighs about 20 grams and commonly provides around 52 calories and 12–13 grams of sugar.

That does not make maple syrup a low-sugar food. It simply means a comparable spoonful is somewhat less concentrated.

Minor nutrients are often used to market one option as healthier. Maple syrup can provide manganese and riboflavin, while honey contains organic acids and various phenolic compounds. Those are real differences, but typical serving sizes are small and both products are used mainly as sweeteners. Choosing one for flavor and using a modest amount makes more sense than increasing the serving in order to obtain trace minerals or antioxidants.

Each sweetener brings different minor compounds

Honey contains organic acids, aromas, and plant compounds that vary widely with floral source. Maple syrup supplies manganese, riboflavin, and characteristic phenolic compounds. Those differences are interesting, but both foods still function primarily as added-sugar sweeteners in the diet.

From a dietary perspective, both count as concentrated sources of sugar. Replacing honey with maple syrup does not automatically turn a sweet breakfast into a low-sugar meal. A few fewer calories per tablespoon can matter if the portion stays the same, but that difference disappears quickly if the milder flavor leads you to pour more. How the product is actually used is part of the nutritional comparison.

Flavor can matter more than a small numerical edge

Honey can be intensely floral; maple syrup brings toasted, caramel-like notes. If a stronger flavor lets you enjoy a recipe with less sweetener, the amount you actually pour may matter more than the modest calorie difference between two fixed spoonfuls.

If your only criterion is lower sugar and calories, pure maple syrup is usually lower than honey. Portion size still determines the real intake.

If your only question is which usually contains less sugar and fewer calories at the same weight or volume, pure maple syrup generally comes out lower. If you are choosing what to buy, flavor, cost, sourcing, and recipe use may matter just as much. Measuring instead of pouring straight from the bottle gives you more control over intake. That practical habit usually matters more than trying to crown one sweetener the “healthy” winner.

faq.question: Which has more sugar, honey or maple syrup?
faq.answer: Honey. It contains about 82 g sugar per 100 g, compared with roughly 60–67 g for pure maple syrup.

faq.question: Which has more calories?
faq.answer: Honey is about 304 calories per 100 g versus roughly 260 calories for maple syrup.

faq.question: Is maple syrup low in sugar?
faq.answer: No. It is lower than honey by weight, but it is still a concentrated added-sugar sweetener.
